lignes.texte: Jaclyn Bjorklund’s teeth started falling out sometime in 2023.
It all stemmed from violent, near-constant vomiting. That started after more than a year
on a drug her doctor prescribed for weight loss. She was hospitalized more than once,
and that year, she became one of the first people in the country to sue over it.
Today, her case is one of thousands. The drug was
semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for diabetes, Wegovy for weight loss.
By now, everybody already knows the basic deal. If you've got money to burn, you don't have to be fat
anymore. What most people never ask is what their money is really buying. What is inside the shot.
So today, we're breaking down how this drug rewrites a signal between your
gut and your brain, why it took the study of lizard venom to figure out,
and why the fine print turns out to be a lot longer than the hype ever let on.
Every drug has an origin story. Most of them are boring.
This one starts with a segment on daytime
TV that almost nobody remembers watching because most did not.
In February 2021, the Dr. Oz show ran a piece on a new diabetes injection with an
odd side effect. Patients kept losing weight they weren’t trying to lose.
At the time, it barely registered. Semaglutide was a decade-old idea wearing a new brand name,
prescribed by endocrinologists to a few million diabetics,
and about as culturally relevant as a rounding error.
Then, on October 1, 2022, Elon Musk answered a fan’s question on Twitter
about how he’d gotten lean. His answer was fasting and a drug called Wegovy.
One tweet, from one of the most-followed accounts (and soon-to-be-owner) of the platform,
did more for this drug's fame than a decade of clinical trials ever managed. Within about a year,
semaglutide prescriptions had climbed 442 percent, and the word Ozempic stopped being
a drug. By the end of 2023, 1.7% of all Americans had been prescribed a
semaglutide medication that year alone, a 40x increase over the past five years.
Soon, Ozempic and Wegovy became a punchline, a flex, a rumor about your favorite celebrity,
and a diagnosis all rolled into one, depending on who was saying the name and how they meant it.
The money behind that name grew just as fast. In September 2023, Novo Nordisk,
the Danish company that makes both Ozempic and Wegovy, overtook LVMH to become the
most valuable public company in Europe, worth more than the entire Danish economy.
By the end of that year, the company said its drugs had helped some 39 million
people worldwide in six months alone, while obesity-drug sales grew 154% year over year.
Suddenly a pharmaceutical company built on a diabetes injection was outperforming the
luxury goods conglomerate that owns Louis Vuitton.
This wasn’t a fad, and it wasn’t a trick. Semaglutide was the first drug in history
to prove in controlled clinical trials that appetite itself runs on a hormonal signal,
and that if you can control that signal, you can control your hunger.
Demand did what it always does when a drug this good meets a culture this
hungry for a shortcut. By March 2022, Wegovy was formally added to the FDA’s
drug shortage list. Ozempic soon followed. For the actual diabetics this drug was built for,
the shortage meant medication they depended on to manage their blood sugar was suddenly difficult
to reliably obtain. Millions of people without diabetes were now competing for the same pens.
Into that gap walked compounding pharmacies,
some operating legally under the FDA’s own shortage exemption, some not.
And then came the counterfeiters.
Fake Ozempic started to turn up in pharmacies across the United States
and Europe, and in at least one documented case,
patients did not even get a weak knockoff. They got actual insulin, mislabeled as semaglutide,
and ended up hospitalized with seizures and dangerously low blood sugar as a result.
Ultimately, a drug that promised to fix a broken signal in the body ended up exposing a much older
one: Where there’s enough money and convenience on the table, the guardrails come off fast.
But how does it actually work?
Semaglutide drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy hinge on a hormone almost nobody outside a
biochemistry lab has ever heard of: GLP-1, or glugagon-like-peptide-1.
Every time you eat, your guy releases a small burst of it. GLP-1 does three
things simultaneously when that happens. It tells your pancreas to release insulin,
but only when your blood sugar is actually elevated, which is actually a built-in safety
feature that keeps it from crashing your glucose the way some diabetes drugs can. It
also hits receptors on your vagus nerve, the long cable running between your gut and your
brainstem which slows down how fast your stomach empties into the small intestine. And finally,
it makes a little trip to your hypothalamus, the walnut-sized command center that regulates
hunger. Once there, it quiets a set of neurons called NPY-AgRP responsible for
that gnawing feeling of needing to take a bite of everything and anything nearby,
conveniently switching on a different set of receptor neurons which signal fullness.
In other words, GLP-1 is responsible for flipping a switch between two competing
populations of brain cells that have been arguing over your next meal since before you were born.
The catch is that GLP-1 in its natural state barely survives inside you for
very long. An enzyme called DPP-4 is also present, which tears it apart
in about two minutes flat. Sometimes you can blink, and the GLP-1 signal is gone.
Semaglutide is what happens when chemists rebuild the same molecule from scratch,
then armor-plate it for battle in your bloodstream.
It’s about 94% identical to your own GLP-1, but with two amino acids swapped out so DPP-4
can’t get a grip on it. It’s also got this fatty side-chain attached to one of its amino
acids that lets it clamp onto albumin, the most abundant protein in your bloodstream.
Once it’s riding around bound to albumin, it’s essentially invisible to the enzymes
that would normally destroy it. That’s how you get a signal that used to last
two minutes suddenly lasting about a week. With just one injection,
your hypothalamus can spend the next seven days being told, on a loop,
that the fuel crisis is over. No more late night crash outs at the fast food drive through window.
That’s the science of everything on the appetite side. But the stomach side is just as real.
Scintigraphy studies, which is what they call the radioactive tracer that
lets researchers watch food moving through someone’s gut in real time,
have found that 37% of people on long-acting semaglutide still had measurable food sitting
in their stomachs four hours after eating while the placebo group had none.
With semaglutide, food is both less appealing and physically packed longer,
which is a big part of why fullness lasts so long after a meal. That is also, not coincidentally,
why nausea is the most common complaint among new users. It might feel like you’re imagining
that queasy, overfull feeling, but your stomach is genuinely moving slower than it’s built to.
So many people’s first weeks on this drug feel miserable for a reason. The dosing
schedule is akin to damage control. Every semaglutide prescription starts absurdly low,
around 0.25 milligrams a week, which is a fraction of the dose that actually
produces meaningful weight loss. This climbs slowly over the next four to
five months from 0.25 to 0.5 to 1 to 1.7 to a maintenance dose of 2.4 milligrams.
The crawl is a calculated necessity, since the body’s GLP-1 receptors and
the gut’s tolerance for delayed gastric emptying need time to adjust to a signal
running at that intensity. If you were to jump straight to the therapeutic dose,
the nausea and vomiting would become severe enough that most people would simply quit.
The data on this is stark. When a diabetes population pilot study tested semaglutide
dosing levels head-to-head in an eight week ramp up versus sixteen weeks, they found the
rush group quit because of nausea 20% of the time. In the slower group, barely 2% bailed.
Both groups ended up at the same dose, with the same results, one just calmer about getting there.
So the nausea you get on semaglutide is basically your body’s way of giving you
a speeding ticket. Slam your foot on the gas and tell your body it will never starve again faster
than it’s built to process, and it fights back the only way it knows how. Ease off, give it a
few months to adjust rather than a few weeks, and most people barely feel the climb at all.
When you put all three mechanisms together–the brain stopping to
signal hunger, the stomach that stops emptying itself quickly,
and a reward system that stops caring, you get a drug that can quietly rewrite the
actual biological conversations that enabled someone to become obese in the first place.
An elegant solution to be sure, but semaglutide’s origins are less so.
Somewhere in the Sonoran desert, there’s a lizard that eats five or
six times a year and considers that a perfectly reasonable schedule.
That’s because the Gila monster spends over 90% of its life doing absolutely nothing
buried underground. Laying motionless, it lives off one enormous meal for months at a stretch,
or about 4-5 per year. And somehow throughout this process, it never
crashes its blood sugar in the way a human would after skipping lunch twice in a row.
For decades nobody thought the fact was useful for anything except impressing people at parties
or possibly winning a round of Jeopardy under the category, “Ozempic Origins.”
Then, in the early 1990s, an endocrinologist named Dr. John Eng got curious about the why.
Eng worked at the Bronx VA Medical Center, and he’d trained under Rosalyn Yalow,
a Nobel laureate who’d invented a technique for detecting microscopic traces of hormones in blood.
Eng turned that same tool on Gila monster saliva in the hopes of figuring out if whatever let
this lizard skip meals for months without consequence might be doing something worth
understanding. His collaborator, Dr. Jean-Pierre Raufman, handled the unglamorous part–driving
test tubes from Brooklyn to the Bronx in his Toyota Camry, sometimes several times a week,
for a project he'd later describe as basically a fishing expedition. Nobody involved thought
they were building a blockbuster. They were just chasing a strange animal fact wherever it led.
And in 1992, it actually led somewhere. Eng isolated a new peptide from the venom,
a 39-amino-acid molecule he named exendin-4.
Structurally, it was about 53 percent identical to a human hormone called GLP-1 but with one
critical difference. Human GLP-1 breaks down in the bloodstream in roughly a minute. Exendin-4
kept working for hours. The lizard, it turned out, was walking around with a naturally slow-release
version of the exact hormone that would eventually fill an entire aisle of your pharmacy.
The story probably should have ended there. But Eng brought the discovery
to the VA expecting some interest in patenting it. No doing. Since lizard
venom wasn’t technically combat related, it wasn’t their commercial concern.
He spent the next few years pitching pharmaceutical companies who mostly
scratched their heads and passed. Peptide drugs had a reputation in the 1990s for
being fragile and expensive to manufacture, which was ironically the exact same problem
exendin-4's slow decay rate happened to solve. Nobody made that connection for years.
Eventually, a small San Diego biotech company took a punt on Eng’s idea. It nearly sank the
company. Burning through its funding for years with nothing to put onto the market,
by 2002 Amylin Pharmaceuticals had roughly one year of cash left before
Eli Lilly stepped in with a $350 million partnership that kept the
lights on. That deal is the reason any of this ever reached a pharmacy shelf.
In 2005, the FDA approved the result, known as Byetta, the first GLP-1 drug in history.
It required two injections per day, every day, and nearly half of trial patients dealt with nausea.
Byetta wasn’t a big hit, and it showed in how few patients actually stuck with it long-term.
The real bottleneck was the clock. Every improvement after Byetta was a fight against
that same two-minute decay rate GLP-1 has always had. Novo Nordisk got it to once a day in 2010,
with a drug called Victoza. In 2017, they cracked once a week entirely,
using a fatty molecular anchor that let the hormone hitch a ride on a
blood protein instead of getting torn apart on its own. That drug is the one you've actually
heard of. They called it semaglutide. They branded it Ozempic and Wegovy.
And so it took the better part of twenty-five years to get from lizard
peptides to “everyone knows at least one person on this drug.” Overnight success,
as usual, took a quarter century to build.
But after all of the effort it took to make GLP-1 a reality,
was it even in a place where cardiologists and medical doctors could take it seriously?
Let’s put that another way. Weight loss alone has never been that impressive
of a marker as a drug passes through its clinical trials. Plenty of interventions
can shrink a waistline without changing a single outcome that actually matters,
like whether a person will survive into the next decade. In other words,
Semaglutide had to clear a much higher bar than whether it moved the scale for its users or not.
And as it turns out, it does. Here’s what the data actually shows.
In the STEP trials that actually got semaglutide approved for weight loss
under the brand name Wegovy, participants lost an average
of about 15 percent of their total body weight over roughly a year and a half.
For a 220 pound person, that’s over 30 pounds shed from a once weekly injection,
all without a single trip to the gym or calorie tracked.
Compare that to the track record of basically every other diet intervention before this,
which all topped off at around 3 to 5%,
and even that modest number would almost always creep back after a couple of years.
In that context, semaglutide started to look like a different category of result entirely.
What actually got cardiologists paying attention was a separate trial called SELECT,
which followed over 17,600 people who already had cardiovascular disease and
were overweight or obese, but not diabetic. These were people with real, measurable risk
of a heart attack or stroke. In that group, semaglutide cut their composite risk by 20%.
In that specific trial, it’s worth mentioning that the weight loss averaged lower than the
STEP trial’s 15%, but that’s because SELECT wasn’t optimized for weight loss but rather
testing whether the drug protected the heart independent of how much weight came off.
And the answer was yes. This was the first time a weight-loss adjacent drug
had ever proven that it could reduce actual cardiac events.
The side-effect nobody anticipated but patients started reporting before researchers had
even coined a term for it was that their “food noise” had gone down. The constant
low-grade mental static telling you to eat something, wondering what’s in the fridge,
doing all this despite you having finished your last meal within the last hour suddenly
started to stop being generated in the first place. This tracks with
what’s actually happening in the brain; GLP-1 receptors sit in the same reward circuitry,
which is the same real estate involved in cravings for nicotine and alcohol, not just food.
That’s led to one of the stranger side stories in the whole saga. A placebo-controlled trial
testing semaglutide specifically for alcohol use disorder found it actually reduced weekly
cravings, average drinks per drinking day, and heavy drinking days, compared to placebo.
Separate research on smokers found people on semaglutide cut their cigarettes per
day significantly more than people who weren't.
Nobody built this drug to treat addiction. It was designed to talk to a hunger signal, and
it turned out that same signal has its fingers in a lot more of your impulses than anyone expected.
It didn’t stop at hearts and cravings either. A separate trial called FLOW
followed people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease–the same
population staring down dialysis in the face–and found semaglutide
cut the risk of major kidney events, cardiovascular events, and death by 24%.
That trial got stopped early, but not because anything went wrong.
The research team simply felt the benefits were so obvious that continuing to give half
the participants a placebo started to look unethical.
And what about knee-pain, of all things? In a trial of 407 people with both obesity and
knee osteoarthritis, the semaglutide group reported significantly more
relief on a standard osteoarthritis pain scale. Some of that is simple physics;
less physical weight means less load on a joint that’s been grinding under it for years.
But researchers also suspect part of it comes from semaglutide’s effect on
inflammation throughout the body more so than the mechanical math of pounds on cartilage.
By this point, a pattern should start to appear. This all started as a once-weekly
diabetes shot. It’s ended up touching the heart, the kidneys, the joints,
and the reward pathways that drive addiction. Five completely different
organ systems affected by one hormone few people had heard of a decade ago.
Now, before this turns into an infomercial you should know that gambling gets mentioned a lot
in this curing of vices conversation too. That’s worth being honest about up front. It’s all mostly
theoretical, extrapolated conclusions from the same shared reward-pathway biology from earlier.
None of that is backed by clinical trials the way smoking and alcohol are. So if someone
you know tells you that semaglutide can cure gambling, they’re a few years ahead of the data.
Regardless, put it all together and you’ve got a drug that does far more than anyone
would have originally bet. Which is exactly the kind of result that should also make you
suspicious. Nothing this good comes without risks. And semaglutide doesn’t, either.
Every one of the aforementioned wins comes with an asterisk attached;
now it’s time to actually read the fine print.
Start with muscle. When your body is told repeatedly that a famine has arrived and
it’s time to burn the reserves, it doesn't neatly sort fat from muscle on the way out.
Research presented at the Endocrine Society’s 2025 meeting found that roughly 40% of the weight
people lose on semaglutide is lean mass. Muscle, in other words, not fat. And they added that older
adults, women, and people eating less protein were at the highest risk of losing more of it.
40% isn’t a fixed cost, either. The same research found that people who
ate more protein while on the drug held onto significantly more muscle.
In other words, semaglutide will happily burn through your muscle
right alongside the fat reserves if you let it. Whether it actually does comes
down to what you’re doing at the dinner table and the gym, not the drug itself.
This is also, in large part, where “Ozempic face” comes from. Lose fat and muscle from
your face at the same time you’re losing it everywhere else, and skin that used to have
volume underneath it just doesn’t anymore. That’s what rapid weight loss has always done to a face,
and semaglutide just made rapid weight loss common enough that people started needing a name for it.
So what happens when you stop the injections? The same as what tends to happen when you stop
dieting or exercising. Clinical follow-up data on people who discontinued semaglutide found that
two-thirds of people had stopped taking GLP-1 drugs within a year. Even with healthy habits,
most people who stop are shown to regain roughly half to two-thirds of their weight back.
Real world data pulled from electronic health records paint a slightly less grim picture,
with a meaningful share of people holding steady or continuing to lose even after stopping. But
the core trial finding stands: for most people, the injections are just like paying rent. Stop
paying it, and the hunger you outsourced to a weekly injection comes back to collect.
On the gastrointestinal side, the drug’s reputation starts to get genuinely
ugly. Slowing gastric emptying is the whole point of the mechanism, but push that too far
in the wrong place and you get gastroparesis, a stomach that essentially stops emptying at all.
More than 31 million Americans, or about 12% of all adults, are currently on a GLP-1 drug,
according to health policy nonprofit KFF.
Out of that enormous population, a fraction of at least 4,400 people have now filed lawsuits
alleging the drugmakers did not adequately warn them what they were signing up for.
75% of these allege gastroparesis, with others claiming intestinal blockages, gallbladder
injuries, gangrenous tissue, chronic acid reflux, abdominal pain and related complications.
Another newer finding that hasn’t made it into most of the celebrity coverage yet either is
that in June 2025, European regulators added a rare but serious vision condition called NAION
to the official Ozempic label. NAION is a sudden, often permanent vision loss. It’s rare. But Todd
Engel found out the hard way that a vague warning on a drug label could mean something much worse.
Four months into taking Ozempic for his diabetes, the Maryland truck driver woke
up one December morning and couldn’t see out of one eye. Doctors diagnosed him with NAION,
sometimes called an eye stroke which stems from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve.
Ten months later, he woke up again, turned to his wife,
and told her the other eye had gone dark too.
Engel is now legally blind. He’d lost his commercial license, his job,
and the ability to watch his grandkids play baseball. This type of injury was enough for
European regulators to add NAION to Ozempic and Wegovy's labels in 2025,
warning it may affect up to 1 in 10,000 patients. American labels still don't mention it by name.
Then there’s JoHelen McClain, a 72-year-old Oklahoma real estate agent who'd lost 40 pounds on
Wegovy with barely any of the nausea she'd braced herself for. In March of 2024, she was driving her
granddaughter home from a softball game when they both heard a loud pop, like a balloon bursting.
It was her colon rupturing with no warning symptoms beforehand, not even constipation.
Surgeons removed a large portion of her colon as she spent five days in the ICU
fighting sepsis. She now lives with a permanent colostomy bag.
Then there’s the case that might be hardest to hear.
Robin Smith started Mounjaro in Louisiana in the fall of 2022
and lost over 80 pounds with barely any side effects until the vomiting started.
By the time her family got her to a hospital, doctors diagnosed her with gastroparesis,
and then something rarer: Wernicke's encephalopathy, a brain disorder triggered
by a vitamin B1 deficiency, often seen in cases of severe malnutrition. The damage
didn't reverse. Her husband describes coming home to a wife who sometimes doesn't recognize
him anymore. The weight has come back, but the woman he married, in some ways, has not.
The honest take is that semaglutide drugs and GLP-1s work well for most people. It rewrites
a broken hunger signal and for millions of people, that has been genuinely life-changing.
But the drug asks something of you in return. It asks for your muscle,
if you’re not paying attention. It asks for your comfort, if you’re
prone to nausea. And it asks for your money, indefinitely, if you want to keep the results.
For the overwhelming majority of the 31 million people on these drugs, the trade
is worth it. A smaller group ends up paying a steeper, stranger bill than they signed up for,
and they rarely find out which group they're in until the invoice actually arrives.
But semaglutide was just the first drop in the avalanche of weight loss products
making their way onto the market. Click the video on screen to learn about Retatrutide,
a peptide that is making semaglutide look like ancient medicine. Thanks for
watching, and subscribe to keep learning more about peptides.
